name: Abu Dhabi
summary: Operating as the Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM), this jurisdiction uses the direct application of English common law and provides a flexible, risk-based captive framework. It offers a dedicated rulebook and a streamlined application process with four distinct classes of captive insurers to meet varied business needs. A major benefit is the 0% tax environment guaranteed until 2065, along with the ability to outsource all management functions to ADGM-authorized managers.
tax_notes: 0% tax until 2065; 5% VAT may apply

name: Alabama
summary: Alabama positions itself at the forefront of the industry by offering innovative features like a 60-day provisional license and the ability to form as any entity allowed under law, including Series LLCs. Legislation enacted in 2006 was significantly updated in 2016 to modernize the Alabama Captive Act and enhance competitiveness. The state is active in advocacy through the Alabama Captive Insurance Association and offers prorated premium taxes in the first year.
tax_notes: $100,000 maximum cap; no tax on dormant captives

name: Alberta
summary: Alberta enacted dedicated captive insurance legislation under the Captive Insurance Companies Act (SA 2021, c. C-2.4), which came into force on July 1, 2022, making it the second Canadian province with a standalone captive statute. Administered by the Alberta Superintendent of Insurance (Treasury Board and Finance), the regime authorizes pure, association, and sophisticated insured captives—formed as either corporations or limited partnerships—as well as redomestication of foreign captives. Driven by strong demand from the energy, natural resource, and commercial sectors, along with Canada's lowest provincial corporate income tax rate (8%) and streamlined 6-week licensing, Alberta has rapidly expanded its captive insurance sector.
legislation: Captive Insurance Companies Act, SA 2021, c. C-2.4 (in force July 1, 2022) & Captive Insurance Companies Regulation, Alta. Reg. 100/2022
applicable_legislation: Captive Insurance Companies Act (SA 2021, c. C-2.4); Captive Insurance Companies Regulation (Alta. Reg. 100/2022); Captive Insurance Companies (Prescribed Enactments) Regulation (Alta. Reg. 103/2022); Fees Under the Captive Insurance Companies Act Order (Ministerial Order 14/2022); Classes of Insurance Regulation (Alta. Reg. 144/2011); Recovery of Insurance Administration Costs Regulation (Alta. Reg. 102/2022); Insurance Enforcement and Administration Regulation (Alta. Reg. 101/2022); Business Corporations Act (RSA 2000, c. B-9); Partnership Act (RSA 2000, c. P-3); Alberta Corporate Tax Act (RSA 2000, c. A-15).

min_capital.Association Captive: CAD 500,000 minimum base capital (or greater of formulaic revenue/claims thresholds or actuary-proposed risk-based amount; subject to Superintendent's determination)
min_capital.Sophisticated Insured Captive: CAD 500,000 minimum base capital (insureds must demonstrate insurance expertise and pay at least CAD 500,000 in aggregate annual premiums; subject to Superintendent's determination)

tax_notes: Subject to federal and provincial corporate income tax (8% Alberta general corporate tax rate) and Alberta insurance premiums tax under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (3% on life, accident and sickness insurance; 4% on property, casualty and other insurance contracts on Alberta risks).

fees.premium_tax_rate: 3% on life, accident and sickness insurance premiums; 4% on property and casualty and all other insurance contracts on risks insured in Alberta (under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act). 8% provincial corporate income tax rate.

annual_filing_requirements: Electronic filing via IRIS required: Captive Annual Return Template and Signed Affidavit within 60 days after calendar year-end; Consolidated Audited Financial Statements (under IFRS 17), Auditor's Report, and Appointed Actuary's Report within 180 days after fiscal year-end; Alberta Premium Tax Return by May 15; Annual Licence Renewal by November 30; monthly Anti-Terrorism Financing Report by the 15th of each month. Principal place of business and records must be maintained in Alberta.

name: Anguilla
summary: Anguilla's Insurance Act provides a comprehensive framework for domestic, offshore, and captive insurance, notably including a specific 2018 provision for producer-affiliated reinsurance companies. The domicile offers five sub-categories of Class B licenses, ranging from unrestricted foreign business to single-owner captives. Unless maintaining a permanent local staff, insurers are required to appoint a licensed insurance manager.
tax_notes: Tax-neutral structures for Class B insurers

name: Arizona
summary: Established in 2002, Arizona is a mature and proven domicile supported by a stable regulatory team and a well-established network of local service providers. The state is highly competitive due to the absence of insurance premium taxes and state/local income taxes for most licensed captives. It provides an electronic filing portal and a cost-effective application process, licensing varied structures including agency and branch captives.
tax_notes: No premium or state income taxes; flat annual license fee

name: Arkansas
summary: Arkansas aggressively recruits captives by refining its laws, including major changes in 2017 and 2019 that reduced capital requirements and welcomed RRGs. It is recognized as one of the most cost-effective domiciles, featuring low application and license fees and a $100,000 tax liability cap. The Arkansas Insurance Department offers no-cost preliminary analyses for companies considering captive formation.
tax_notes: $100,000 maximum annual tax liability

name: Aruba
summary: Aruba offers a safe and stable environment for financial services with an international legal framework overseen by the Central Bank of Aruba. Captives are defined as businesses insuring risks originating almost exclusively from shareholders, affiliates, or joint venture participants. Operations must maintain an office in Aruba for financial administration and have at least one managing director residing on the island.

min_capital.General: Subject to Central Bank review and actuarial report

tax_notes: Requires annual audited financial statements

name: Bahrain
summary: Bahrain serves as a regional base for international insurers, with a sector regulated by the Central Bank of Bahrain (CBB) as a single regulator since 2002. The CBB differentiates between captive and commercial insurers, offering lower capital and solvency requirements for captives provided they do not include third-party liability risks. The domicile is supported by a large pool of brokers, actuaries, and insurance managers.

min_capital.Captive: Risk-based; lower than traditional insurers unless third-party liability is involved

tax_notes: Competitive regulatory environment

name: Barbados
summary: Barbados licenses insurers under the Insurance Act, Cap. 310. The Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2018-52 commenced on 1 January 2019, created three licence classes, and repealed the Exempt Insurance Act, Cap. 308A. A Class 1 licensee is an insurance company that underwrites related-party business. A Class 2 licensee includes an insurance company that underwrites third-party risks, and Class 3 covers insurance intermediaries, managers, and holding companies. The Financial Services Commission supervises the sector under the Financial Services Commission Act, 2010-21. The Commission's homepage reported 176 Class 1 licensees at 31 December 2025, compared with 175 at 31 December 2024. It reported 121 Class 2 licensees at 31 December 2025, of which 21 had direct exposure to the Barbadian public, and 815 Class 3 licensees. Class 1 is the related-party population. The Commission does not publish a pure-versus-group split, a cell count, or 2025 figures for new and surrendered Class 1 licences.
legislation: Insurance Act, Cap. 310, as amended by the Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2018-52 (commenced 1 January 2019)
applicable_legislation: Insurance Act, Cap. 310; Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2018-52, which commenced on 1 January 2019 and repealed the Exempt Insurance Act, Cap. 308A; Financial Services Commission Act, 2010-21. Minimum capital and solvency for Class 1 and Class 2 insurers are set out in the Commission's capital and solvency appendix.

An equivalent sum in another currency is allowed if the Commission approves it. Capital must be fully paid up in cash.
min_capital.Class 1 or Class 2, risks and premiums i: BDS $3,000,000 long-term; BDS $3,000,000 general; BDS $5,000,000 long-term and general; BDS $1,000,000 motor vehicle only; BDS $1,000,000 industrial life.
min_capital.Segregated cell company, Barbados reinsu: A Class 1 or Class 2 segregated cell company licensed to carry on reinsurance of risks located in Barbados, with premiums originating in Barbados, must have aggregate paid-up capital of BDS $3,000,000, and each cell must have minimum paid-up capital of BDS $500,000.
min_capital.Solvency, risks and premiums outside Bar: In the first financial year, assets must exceed liabilities by BDS $250,000. After that year, assets must exceed liabilities by BDS $250,000 if the preceding year's premium income did not exceed BDS $1,500,000; by one-fifth of that premium income if it exceeded BDS $1,500,000 but did not exceed BDS $10,000,000; or by BDS $2,000,000 plus one-tenth of the amount by which premium income exceeded BDS $10,000,000.

The same table still shows 0 percent for exempt insurance companies and 0.35 percent for qualifying insurance companies that were licensed under the Insurance Act, Cap. 310 and carrying on life insurance business before 17 October 2017. No separate captive premium tax was stated on the Revenue Authority corporations page or the Commission pages used.

fees.annual_fees: The annual fee in Part I of the Commission's fees schedule is payable by 31 January each year. The dollar amounts in that schedule are not restated because the published PDF did not yield a reliable text extraction.
fees.premium_tax_rate: Corporate income tax of 0 percent for Class 1, 2 percent for Class 2, and 2 percent for Class 3. No separate premium-tax rate was published on the pages used.

annual_filing_requirements: The annual fee in Part I of the Commission's fees schedule is payable by 31 January. A current deadline for audited financial statements was not confirmed on the Commission pages reviewed.

name: Bermuda
summary: Bermuda's captive classes are supervised by the Bermuda Monetary Authority under the Insurance Act 1978. Class 1 is a single-parent general captive writing only the risks of its owners and their affiliates. Class 2 covers multi-owner captives and captives writing no more than 20 percent of net premiums from unrelated risks. Class 3 covers captives writing more than 20 percent, and up to 49 percent, of net premiums from unrelated risks, together with certain third-party writers that are not commercial Class 3A, 3B, or 4 insurers. Class A and Class B are the long-term equivalents of Class 1 and Class 2. The Authority's 2025 annual report gives 2025 register counts of 159 Class 1, 244 Class 2, 180 Class 3, 12 Class A, and 13 Class B insurers, 608 in those captive classes. The 2024 column of the same table is 632 and matches the report's market statistics for the year ended 31 December 2024. Single-parent captives are the Class 1 and Class A counts, 171 in the 2025 column, which is the same pairing the report used for its 31 December 2024 company-type table. Class 3, 180, is the third-party captive category. Class 2 and Class B together are 257 and mix multi-owner captives with captives writing up to 20 percent unrelated premiums, so that pair is not stored as a group-captive count. New captive-class registrations in the 2025 column were 2 Class 1, 5 Class 2, 1 Class 3, 1 Class A, and no Class B, 9 in total. The report does not publish surrenders. Its 2023 captive insight report, published in December 2025, said segregated and incorporated segregated accounts were in excess of 2,000 and that 15 percent of captive-market companies operated as segregated accounts or incorporated segregated accounts companies. That report does not give an exact cell count, and the 2025 annual report does not update it.
legislation: Insurance Act 1978, and the Insurance Returns and Solvency Regulations 1980
applicable_legislation: Insurance Act 1978, including section 17 on statutory financial statements and section 18 on statutory financial returns; Insurance Returns and Solvency Regulations 1980, Schedule I (general-business solvency margin) and Schedule II (long-term minimum margin of solvency); Bermuda Monetary Authority Act 1969, Fourth Schedule, for fees effective 1 January 2026; Corporate Income Tax Act 2023.

min_capital.Class 1: Minimum capital and surplus at least equal to the minimum solvency margin, the greater of a premium-based formula and a reserve-based formula, subject to a $120,000 floor.
min_capital.Class 2: Minimum capital and surplus at least equal to the minimum solvency margin, subject to a $250,000 floor.
min_capital.Class 3: Minimum capital and surplus at least equal to the minimum solvency margin, subject to a $1,000,000 floor.
min_capital.Class A: Long-term single-parent captives maintain minimum capital and surplus at least equal to an asset-based formula, subject to a $120,000 floor.
min_capital.Class B: Long-term multi-owner captives, and long-term captives writing no more than 20 percent of net premiums from unrelated risks, maintain minimum capital and surplus at least equal to an asset-based formula, subject to a $250,000 floor.

tax_notes: The Insurance Act fee schedule does not impose a premium tax. Captive regulatory cost is the Bermuda Monetary Authority licence fee. The Corporate Income Tax Act 2023 charges Bermuda corporate income tax to Bermuda constituent entities of an in-scope multinational group for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025. The Government of Bermuda describes that regime as its implementation of the OECD Pillar II 15 percent minimum tax for multinational groups with annual revenue of EUR 750 million or more. Captives that are not constituent entities of an in-scope group are outside that tax.
types_allowed: Class 2 multi-owner general captives and captives writing up to 20 percent unrelated net premiums
Class 3 captives writing more than 20 percent and up to 49 percent unrelated net premiums
Class B multi-owner long-term captives and long-term captives writing up to 20 percent unrelated net premiums
Segregated accounts companies and incorporated segregated accounts companies

fees.licensing_incorporation: 2026 registration fees in the Bermuda Monetary Authority fee schedule, effective 1 January 2026: Class 1 general business $2,250; Class 2 general business $4,375; Class 3 general business $17,800 where expected gross premium does not exceed $5 million, then $19,800, $22,550, $25,920, and $30,000 at the published premium bands; Class A $13,570; Class B $13,570.
fees.annual_fees: 2026 annual fees, also effective 1 January 2026, match those registration amounts for Class 1 ($2,250), Class 2 ($4,375), Class 3 ($17,800 to $30,000 by gross premium written), Class A ($13,570), and Class B ($13,570). For a segregated accounts company the premium measure combines the general account and the segregated accounts. Annual fees cancelled by deregistration, discontinuance, or merger before 31 March are pro-rated; otherwise the full annual fee is due.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax is imposed by the Insurance Act fee schedule. Bermuda corporate income tax applies only to Bermuda constituent entities of an in-scope multinational group, for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025. The Government describes the rate as the OECD Pillar II 15 percent minimum for groups with annual revenue of EUR 750 million or more.

annual_filing_requirements: Under section 17 of the Insurance Act 1978, a Class 1, Class 2, or Class 3 insurer that is not also Class C, D, or E, and a Class A or Class B insurer, files statutory financial statements within six months after the financial year-end, or within a longer period of up to nine months that the Authority allows on application. The statutory financial return under section 18 is filed at the same time. A loss-reserve specialist's opinion is required annually for a Class 3 insurer and every third year for a Class 2 insurer. The Act does not state that opinion for a Class 1 insurer.

name: British Columbia
summary: British Columbia enacted Canada's first dedicated captive insurance statute in 1987 under the Insurance (Captive Company) Act (RSBC 1996, c. 227) and remains one of two Canadian provinces with standalone captive legislation alongside Alberta. Regulated by the BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA), which succeeded the Financial Institutions Commission (FICOM) in 2019, it permits pure, association, and sophisticated insured captives—the latter requiring insureds to have aggregate annual insurance premiums of at least CAD 500,000. Captives can write nearly all classes of insurance or reinsurance (excluding direct surety and non-fleet automobile) and require a minimum of CAD 200,000 in shareholders' equity and CAD 100,000 in reserves.

name: British Virgin Islands
summary: The BVI offers a seamless approach to captive formation, leveraging a long tenure in corporate domiciliation and a deep cadre of professional expertise. It licenses various captive categories, including Category E for pure captives and segregated portfolio companies that allow independent underwriting for owners. There is no corporate income tax in the BVI, and capital requirements vary based on the insurance line.
tax_notes: No corporate income tax

name: Cayman Islands
summary: The Cayman Islands is the world's second-largest captive domicile and the leading domicile for healthcare captives, regulated by the Cayman Islands Monetary Authority (CIMA) under the Insurance Act, 2010, as amended. International insurers are licensed as Class B (B(i) where at least 95 percent of net premiums come from related business, B(ii) where more than 50 percent are related, and B(iii) where 50 percent or less are related), Class C (fully collateralised insurance-linked structures) or Class D (open-market reinsurance). As of Q3 2026, CIMA reported 720 Class B, C and D insurers, writing US$62.3 billion of premium and holding US$202.9 billion of assets. Of that population, 337 were categorised as pure captives and 149 as group captives. Medical malpractice was the primary class of 127 licensees, and North America accounted for 632 licensees (88 percent). Class B segregated portfolio companies numbered 177, with 634 segregated portfolios and 68 portfolio insurance companies; those counts sit inside the 720 and are not additional licensees. In 2025 CIMA issued 42 international licences and cancelled 19. Through the 2026 year to date, issues and cancellations were 28 and 28, leaving the international total at 720. Every captive must appoint a licensed local insurance manager. CIMA states that a complete Class B or Class C application takes six to eight weeks. The Islands levy an annual licence fee rather than a premium tax, and CIMA describes the domicile as having no corporate or personal taxes.

name: China
summary: China's captive sector is primarily focused on pure captives owned by large state-owned or private enterprises with assets exceeding RMB 100 billion. The CBIRC oversees the industry, utilizing the China Risk Oriented Solvency System (C-ROSS) without exemption for captives. There are no specific tax exemptions for captives; they are subject to standard corporate tax rates of 25% and 6% VAT.
tax_notes: 25% Corporate tax; 6% VAT

name: Connecticut
summary: Connecticut, the 'insurance capital of the world,' has modernized its captive laws and application process to offer quick decisions and a risk-based regulatory approach. The state is unique for its concentration of insurtech, commercial insurers, and experienced regulators. It offers first-year premium tax credits of $7,500 and avoids the use of outside consultants to keep formation costs low.
tax_notes: $7,500 minimum; $200,000 maximum tax

name: Cook Islands
summary: The Cook Islands enacted its Captive Insurance Act in 2013 to regulate business conducted both inside and outside its borders by international companies. As of January 2022, companies are subject to a 20% tax on worldwide income to comply with EU standards and avoid non-cooperative listing. Domicile requirements include audited annual accounts filed with the Financial Supervisory Commission.
tax_notes: 20% worldwide income tax (as of 2022)

name: Delaware
summary: Delaware licenses captives under Title 18, Chapter 69 of the Delaware Code. The Department of Insurance Bureau of Captive and Financial Insurance Products administers the chapter, and the Bureau's welcome page identifies House Bill 218 (2005) as the statute that modernized the law. The Department's 2025 year-in-review reported 638 captives after 51 new licences that year. Minimum capital and surplus is $250,000 for a pure, agency, branch or special purpose captive, $500,000 for an industrial insured captive or a sponsored captive, $750,000 for an association captive, and $1,000,000 for a risk retention group. A series captive's minimum is the amount the Commissioner specifies. Direct premium tax is 0.2 percent, with a $200,000 direct-tax cap, and assumed reinsurance premium tax is 0.1 percent, with a $110,000 cap. The annual minimum is $5,000, or $3,500 for a series captive, and the annual aggregate cap is $200,000. Under § 6914(d) that premium tax is in lieu of other Delaware state and local occupation taxes, other than ad valorem property tax. A conditional certificate of authority is dated the day the Bureau receives the emailed application, if the $3,600 fee arrives within 10 business days.
legislation: Title 18, Delaware Code, Chapter 69 (Captive Insurance Companies); the Bureau identifies House Bill 218 (2005) as the modernizing statute
applicable_legislation: Title 18, Delaware Code, Chapter 69 (Captive Insurance Companies), including § 6902 (definitions), § 6903 (licence application, fees and conditional certificates), § 6905 (minimum capital and surplus), § 6906 (formation), § 6907 (annual reports), § 6914 (tax on premiums) and § 6924 (dormant captive insurance companies). The current text is published on the Delaware Code Online.

Minimum capital is held as cash, an irrevocable letter of credit from an institution chartered, licensed or otherwise authorized to do banking business in Delaware, or another institution or asset the Commissioner approves. Surplus-note proceeds may count if the Commissioner approves the note (§ 6905(c) and (d))

tax_notes: Direct premiums are taxed at 2/10 of 1 percent (0.2 percent), up to $200,000, and assumed reinsurance premiums at 1/10 of 1 percent (0.1 percent), up to $110,000. Premiums already taxed as direct premiums are not taxed again as assumed reinsurance, and no tax is due on annuity consideration. The annual minimum aggregate tax is $5,000, or $3,500 for a series captive. The annual maximum aggregate tax is $200,000, except that series captives formed in the same limited liability company or statutory trust are not aggregated into that cap. A captive that employs at least 25 qualified full-time individuals in Delaware pays $50,000 if the formula would otherwise exceed that amount. Tax is due by 15 April. Under § 6914(d) this premium tax is all of the tax collectible under Delaware law from a captive, and no other occupation tax is levied by the State or by a county, city or municipality, except ad valorem taxes on real and personal property used in the production of income. A dormant captive is not liable for the premium tax. There is no separate Delaware corporate income tax on captives in Chapter 69.
contact_name: Stephen Taylor, Director, Bureau of Captive & Financial Insurance Products

fees.licensing_incorporation: Nonrefundable application fee of $300 to review completeness, plus a nonrefundable processing fee of $3,200 (18 Del. C. § 6903(d)). The 2024 Bureau application notice collects $3,500 for a regular application. A conditional certificate adds a $100 fee under § 6903(d)(5); the same 2024 notice collects $3,600 for a conditional application. The annual licence fee for the year of registration is $400.
fees.annual_fees: $400 certificate-of-authority renewal fee, due 15 April, payable with the premium-tax report. From the 2025 premium tax and 2026 renewal, payment may be made through OPTins or by the existing procedure. A dormant captive that has not resumed business after five years pays a renewal fee of $25,000 in the sixth year of dormancy and $5,000 in each year of dormancy after that (§ 6924(g)).
fees.premium_tax_rate: Direct premiums 0.2 percent, maximum $200,000. Assumed reinsurance premiums 0.1 percent, maximum $110,000. Annual minimum aggregate tax $5,000, or $3,500 for a series captive. Annual maximum aggregate tax $200,000. A captive with at least 25 qualified Delaware employees is capped at $50,000. No annuity tax. Dormant captives pay no premium tax.

annual_filing_requirements: Each captive other than a branch captive for which the Commissioner has waived the requirement files a report of financial condition by 15 April, verified by oath of two executive officers or authorized persons, using GAAP unless the Commissioner approves statutory accounting principles or international accounting standards (§ 6907). The Bureau requires the annual report (Form F-1, updated 31 March 2025, for pure captives, core LLCs and series; special purpose financial captives that file NAIC statements are excepted) by 15 April, or within 60 days of fiscal year-end where an alternate year-end is used. Audited financial statements and a statement of actuarial opinion, for captives that retain risk, are due by 30 June. Special purpose financial captives also file quarterly reports with the NAIC and the Bureau by 15 May, 15 August and 15 November. Premium tax and the $400 renewal fee are due by 15 April. Annual reports are emailed to captive@delaware.gov.

captive_administrator.name: Stephen Taylor, Director, Bureau of Captive & Financial Insurance Products, Delaware Department of Insurance

licensing_speed: The 2024 Bureau application notice dates a conditional certificate on the day the emailed application is received, provided the $3,600 fee reaches the Dover accounting office within 10 business days. Only a captive manager that already manages at least two Delaware captives may file a conditional application. In October 2023 the Department said its goal for review of initial application filings is 30 days, down from 45, and that conditional applications received after 1 November are reviewed within 80 days. That 2023 goal is not restated in the 2024 notice or the March 2026 OPTins notice.

regulator.name: Delaware Department of Insurance, Bureau of Captive & Financial Insurance Products

name: District of Columbia
summary: The District of Columbia features a progressive insurance code and a knowledgeable staff specializing in captives and risk retention groups. It offers competitive costs for financial examinations and does not require a local director, though at least one annual board meeting must be facilitated from the district. Examination cycles occur every five years but can be extended upon request.
tax_notes: Favorable examination costs compared to other domiciles

name: Dubai
summary: The Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) is a leading hub for the MEASA region, connecting emerging markets with a proven judicial system and an English common law framework. Regulated by the independent DFSA, the domicile offers 100% digital onboarding and a 0% tax rate on corporate income guaranteed until 2054. It allows for pure, third-party, and association captives with case-by-case flexibility on capital structures.
tax_notes: 0% tax until 2054; waived commercial license fees

name: Federated States of Micronesia
summary: Micronesia enacted its captive law in 2006 specifically to provide Japanese corporations with a conveniently located domicile under a responsive regulatory environment. Captives are required to file audited financial statements that can be prepared under US or Japanese GAAP. Beyond a low 0.05% premium tax, captives also file a simple annual income tax return computed at 21% of net income.
tax_notes: 0.05% premium tax; 21% net income tax

name: Florida
summary: Florida's captive provisions were augmented in 2012 to further specify criteria for formation, capital, and licensure. The state's unique selling point is its relatively low capital requirements across its four main captive types: pure, industrial insured, special purpose, and reinsurance. Interested parties are directed to Chapter 628 of the Florida statutes for detailed variation in requirement by captive type.
tax_notes: Requires annual reporting compliance

name: France
summary: France is a growing challenger in the European market, applying Solvency II regulations to ensure high quality in shareholders and solvency. Domiciling in France allows direct captives to operate across Europe under the Freedom of Service principle. The regulator, ACPR, maintains a dedicated team for captive supervision and emphasizes solid governance structured around '4 eyes' principles.
tax_notes: Freedom of Service access across the EU

name: Georgia
summary: The Georgia Insurance Department provides a healthy regulatory environment for captives, supported by 2018 legislation that improved formation efficiency. Georgia's premium tax structure is tiered and provides for captives under common ownership to be taxed as a single entity. The state emphasizes superior customer service to help its 50+ active captives succeed.
tax_notes: Max tax of $100,000 per year; reinsurance tax may be waived

name: Germany
summary: While not a typical domicile, Germany attracts captives through compliance requirements and the efficiency of sharing staff with parent companies and in-house brokers. Operations are governed by Solvency II and Section 122 VAG, with BaFin withdrawing authorization if eligible funds fall below strict minimums. Minimum capital requirements are calculated based on EU Delegated Regulation 2015/35.
tax_notes: No specific tax exemptions reported

name: Gibraltar
summary: As an onshore domicile for over 50 years, Gibraltar offers captive owners direct access to the UK market under flexible EU-based laws. It features a low flat tax rate of 10% which has been in effect since 2010. While capital requirements can be more onerous than offshore locations, the domicile permits varied structures including protected cell companies and managing general agents.

min_capital.General: More onerous than offshore; varies by structure

tax_notes: 10% across the board tax rate

name: Guam
summary: Guam offers a unique geographical advantage for US-linked business in the Pacific and features 100% tax abatement and rebates for corporate and gross receipts taxes. Legislation enacted in 1996 and subsequent amendments provide an attractive environment for risk management headquarters. Capital and surplus can be held in cash or irrevocable letters of credit approved by the commissioner.
tax_notes: 100% tax rebates for commercial and captive companies

name: Guernsey
summary: Guernsey is a leading captive centre and the jurisdiction that pioneered the protected cell company. The Guernsey Financial Services Commission regulates insurers under the Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended, using its own solvency rules rather than the EU Solvency II standard formula. At 31 December 2025 the Commission reported 196 non-cellular captives, after 8 additions and 9 surrenders in 2025. That 196 is not a total of all captives: of cells reported by type of insurer, 126 were classified as captives, after 13 additions and 9 surrenders. Pure/single-parent and group/association captive structures are permitted; the Commission does not publish a numerical breakdown of those types, a captive-only premium total, or a standard licensing time. At 31 December 2025 the international insurance sector comprised 44 PCCs, 222 PCC cells excluding insurance-linked securities, 14 ICCs and 46 ICC cells. Those PCC and ICC totals cover the wider international insurance sector and are not all captives. The same sector statistics also show 223 companies and 549 entities in total. The latest financial totals, for 2024, were £29.70 billion of gross assets, £12.62 billion of net worth and £5.19 billion of premiums written by international insurers as a whole, not by captives alone. Captive (re)insurers are Category 5 licensees. Category 6, including special purpose insurers and insurance-linked securities, is authorised separately and is not necessarily captive business. The capital floor is £100,000 for general business and £250,000 for long-term business, and the captive prescribed capital requirement is calibrated at a 90 percent confidence level over 12 months. Under the Income Tax (Guernsey) Law, 1975, as amended, and States of Guernsey Revenue Service guidance, company income tax is 0 percent on insurance income that is not domestic business and 10 percent on domestic insurance business. Reinsurance is outside the statutory definition of domestic business. Insurance supervision is carried out by the Banking and Insurance Division; the Commission does not publish a separate current headcount for insurance supervision alone. The Commission regulates insurers and does not administer individual captives. Most international insurers are administered by licensed insurance managers: 23 were authorised at 31 December 2025, and named managers are on the regulated-entities register. The Commission can pre-authorise later protected-cell-company cells on a product or class basis once the company and its first cell are approved, most often for fully collateralised special purpose insurer cells. It does not publish a 48-hour licensing standard. This profile was reviewed by the Commission (Shaun Green, 5 November 2026) against its published insurance statistics.
legislation: Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended, and the Insurance Business (Solvency) Rules and Guidance, 2021
applicable_legislation: Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended; Insurance Managers and Insurance Intermediaries (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002; Insurance Business (Solvency) Rules and Guidance, 2021, including the 2024 amendment to the retail general-business capital floor; Insurance Business Rules and Guidance, 2021; Companies (Guernsey) Law, 2008 (Commission consent to incorporate a protected cell company or an incorporated cell company); Financial Services Commission (Fees and Administrative Penalties) Regulations, 2025; Income Tax (Guernsey) Law, 1975, as amended (company standard rate 0 percent and intermediate rate 10 percent, per States of Guernsey Revenue Service guidance).

min_capital.Category 5 captive, general business: £100,000 capital floor. Paid-up share capital must be at least the capital floor, and minimum shareholders' funds must be at least 75 percent of the capital floor. The minimum capital requirement cannot be below the capital floor. The prescribed capital requirement is set at a 90 percent confidence level over the next 12 months
min_capital.Category 5 captive, long-term business: £250,000 capital floor, with the same paid-up capital, shareholders' funds and 90 percent prescribed-capital tests
min_capital.Protected cell company that does not wri: The capital floor applies to the PCC as a whole. There is no separate capital floor for each cell or for the core. Each cell and the core has a notional minimum capital requirement calculated as if it were a stand-alone insurer, and the PCC minimum is the sum of those amounts, subject to the capital floor

tax_notes: Under the Income Tax (Guernsey) Law, 1975, as amended, and States of Guernsey Revenue Service guidance, the standard company rate of income tax is 0 percent. The 10 percent company intermediate rate applies to income from domestic insurance business, insurance intermediary business and insurance manager business. Insurance income that is not domestic business, including reinsurance (which the Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended, excludes from domestic business), is taxed at 0 percent. Income from Guernsey land and buildings is taxed at 20 percent. Insurance is an economic-substance category for accounting periods after 1 January 2019. Revenue Service company-tax guidance does not state a separate premium-tax rate.
types_allowed: Category 5 captive insurers and reinsurers. Pure/single-parent and group/association structures are permitted; a separate count is not published
Protected cell companies and cells used for captive business
Incorporated cell companies and cells used for captive business
regulator_staff_count: Banking and Insurance Division. No separate current headcount for insurance supervision is published.

fees.licensing_incorporation: Under the Financial Services Commission (Fees and Administrative Penalties) Regulations, 2025, as summarised by the GFSC: Category 5 captive insurer or reinsurer application fee £7,850 for a company, PCC core or ICC core. A Category 5 cell of a PCC or ICC is £2,520. A Category 6 special purpose insurer cell is £110. A pro-rata annual fee is invoiced when the licence is issued.
fees.annual_fees: Due 31 January for licences in effect on 1 January. Category 5 captive insurer or reinsurer, including a PCC core or ICC: £7,850. Category 5 cell: £2,520. Category 6 company: £7,725. Category 6 cell that is not a special purpose insurer: £2,520. Special purpose insurer cell: £110. Dormant cell: £205. Change of general representative: £600. Change of controller: £2,760. Category 6, including special purpose insurers and insurance-linked securities, is a separate licence category and is not necessarily captive business.
fees.premium_tax_rate: Under the Income Tax (Guernsey) Law, 1975, as amended, and States of Guernsey Revenue Service guidance, company income tax is 0 percent on insurance income that is not domestic business and 10 percent on domestic insurance business. That guidance does not state a separate premium-tax rate.

annual_filing_requirements: Licensed insurers must deposit an annual return with the Commission within four months beginning on the close of the financial year (Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended, section 37). The return includes the regulatory solvency assessment. Each insurer must also complete an Own Risk and Solvency Assessment at least annually and submit the resulting Own Solvency Capital Assessment with the annual return. The general representative is responsible for filing. A late return attracts an administrative financial penalty. Licensed insurance managers and insurance intermediaries deposit their annual return within six months of the financial year-end. Guernsey company income tax returns are filed separately with the Revenue Service; the 2025 corporate return is due 30 November 2026.

captive_administrator.name: Licensed insurance managers (23 authorised at 31 December 2025). Named managers are listed on the GFSC regulated-entities register. The Commission is the regulator, not the administrator of individual captives.

licensing_speed: No published standard timeline. PCC cells may be pre-authorised on a product or class basis after the PCC and its first cell are approved; this route is most commonly used for fully collateralised special purpose insurer cells.

name: Hawaii
summary: Hawaii has licensed captive insurers since May 1986 under Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 431, Article 19, administered by the Insurance Division's Captive Insurance Branch. The Division's fact sheet reported 276 captive companies as of 30 September 2026. Licenses are issued in five classes. The statutory floors for unimpaired capital and surplus are $100,000 for a Class 1 pure captive that reinsures only, $250,000 for a Class 2 pure captive that may write direct insurance, and $500,000 for a Class 3 association or risk retention captive and for a Class 4 sponsored captive. Class 5 reinsurance or excess captives, and the security a branch captive posts in Hawaii, are set by the Insurance Commissioner. Premium tax has no minimum and a $200,000 maximum, and it does not apply to premiums already taxed where the risk is located or to reinsurance premiums assumed by the captive. A dormant captive holding a certificate of dormancy maintains at least $25,000 of capital and surplus and is not subject to that tax.
legislation: Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 431, Article 19 (Captive Insurance Companies)
applicable_legislation: Hawaii Revised Statutes Title 24, Chapter 431, Article 19 (Captive Insurance Companies), including §431:19-101 (classes), §431:19-102 (certificate of authority), §431:19-104 (minimum capital and surplus), §431:19-107 (financial statements), §431:19-108 (examinations), §431:19-116 (taxation), and §431:19-117 (dormant captive insurance companies, added by Act 69, Session Laws of Hawaii 2024). License and application fees are set in Hawaii Administrative Rules §16-17-6.

min_capital.Class 1: Not less than $100,000. A Class 1 company is a pure captive licensed to write business only as a reinsurer (HRS §§431:19-101 and 431:19-104).
min_capital.Class 2: Not less than $250,000. A Class 2 company is a pure captive licensed to write direct insurance, or direct insurance and reinsurance.
min_capital.Class 3: Not less than $500,000. A Class 3 company is an association captive or a risk retention captive. Other provisions of Chapter 431 may require more.
min_capital.Class 4: Not less than $500,000. A Class 4 company is a sponsored captive.
min_capital.Class 5: An amount set by the Insurance Commissioner case by case. A Class 5 company is a reinsurance or excess captive licensed under HRS §431:19-111.5.
min_capital.Branch captive: In lieu of the class minimum, the commissioner determines the amount and form of security maintained in Hawaii after considering the risk retained in the state, the outside captive's financial condition, and other security already posted (HRS §431:19-104(c)).
min_capital.Dormant captive: Not less than $25,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus while a certificate of dormancy is in force (HRS §431:19-117).
min_capital.Commissioner discretion: The commissioner sets each captive's required unimpaired capital and surplus after considering the nature and volume of its business. The class amounts are floors. Capital may be held in cash, an irrevocable letter of credit, public obligations, or another form the commissioner approves.

tax_notes: Premium tax under HRS §431:19-116 is paid to the director of finance through the commissioner by March 1. On gross premiums for risks resident, situated, or located in Hawaii, and on risks elsewhere on which no premium tax is otherwise paid, less return premiums and less reinsurance accepted, the rates are 0.25% from $0 to $25 million, 0.15% from more than $25 million to $50 million, 0.05% from more than $50 million to $250 million, and 0% above $250 million. There is no minimum tax. The annual maximum aggregate tax is $200,000. The tax is in lieu of other Hawaii state and county taxes except taxes on real property and on the purchase, use, or ownership of tangible personal property. The Insurance Division states the same rule as a tax on the captive's own premiums only, with no tax on premiums already taxed where the underlying risk is located and no tax on reinsurance premiums assumed by the captive. A dormant captive that holds a certificate of dormancy is not subject to the §431:19-116 tax (HRS §431:19-117).
contact_name: Andrew J. Kurata, Deputy Commissioner and Captive Insurance Administrator
types_allowed: Class 1 pure captives writing reinsurance only
Class 2 pure captives writing direct insurance, or direct insurance and reinsurance
Class 4 sponsored captives, which may use protected cells
Branch captives of an outside captive
Dormant captives holding a certificate of dormancy

fees.licensing_incorporation: $50 initial business-registration incorporation fee and a $1,000 nonrefundable captive application fee. If the commissioner uses an independent advisor to review an application or business-plan amendment, the applicant pays a reasonable fee authorized by the commissioner (HRS §431:19-102; Hawaii Administrative Rules §16-17-6).
fees.annual_fees: $15 annual business-registration fee. The certificate-of-authority renewal, due on or before April 1, is $300 for a Class 1 or Class 2 captive, $500 for a Class 3 captive, and $1,000 for a Class 4 or Class 5 captive (HAR §16-17-6). A certificate of dormancy is renewed every five years for $300 (HRS §431:19-117).
fees.premium_tax_rate: 0.25% on the first $25 million, 0.15% from $25 million to $50 million, 0.05% from $50 million to $250 million, and 0% above $250 million. No minimum tax. Maximum annual tax $200,000. No tax on premiums already taxed where the risk is located, on assumed reinsurance, or on a dormant captive holding a certificate of dormancy.

annual_filing_requirements: A captive other than a risk retention captive files financial statements, prepared on generally accepted accounting principles or another basis the commissioner accepts and audited by an independent certified public accountant or another professional the commissioner accepts, on or before the last day of the sixth month after its fiscal year-end (HRS §431:19-107(a)). A risk retention captive files an NAIC annual statement and a risk-based capital report by March 1 and an audit by June 1. Actuarial opinions on reserves are included with the audited statements, except that a Class 3 company files its actuarial opinion with the annual statement by March 1. The premium-tax statement is due March 1 (HRS §431:19-116). The governing body holds at least one meeting each year in Hawaii, and the captive keeps its principal place of business in the state (HRS §431:19-102). Examinations occur at least once every five years; a risk retention captive is examined no later than three years after formation and at least once every five years after that (HRS §431:19-108). The Captive Insurance Branch requires electronic annual filings to CaptiveInsAnnualFilings@dcca.hawaii.gov. A dormant captive with a certificate of dormancy files a verified report of its financial condition by March 1 and does not file the audited statements required by §431:19-107.

captive_administrator.name: Andrew J. Kurata, Deputy Commissioner and Captive Insurance Administrator

licensing_speed: No published standard timeline. Once issued, a certificate of authority authorizes business until April 1 and may be renewed (HRS §431:19-102).

regulator.name: Hawaii Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, Insurance Division, Captive Insurance Branch

name: Hong Kong
summary: Hong Kong is a leading Asian financial hub that encourages captive establishment through simple tax regimes and targeted concessions for marine and specialty insurance. Since 2013, it has provided a 50% reduction in corporate tax for offshore business, later extended to onshore risks. The Insurance Authority's strategic vision is to build a regional hub through a bespoke regime for insurance-linked securities (ILS).
tax_notes: 16.5% Corporate tax; 50% concession available

name: Illinois
summary: Illinois modernized its Insurance Code in 2018 to lower capital and surplus requirements and filing fees, making the state a more viable captive domicile. The state now allows captives to make loans to affiliates with prior approval and permits captive reinsurance pools. Despite having one of the highest GDPs in the US, Illinois has only recently become an active competitor in the captive space.
tax_notes: $2,000 filing fee (lowered from $7,000)

name: Ireland
summary: Ireland is a global re/insurance center that provides a stable operating environment with direct access to all EEA countries through EU passporting. The Central Bank of Ireland (CBI) applies Solvency II proportionately through its PRISM system, which allows captives to have fewer directors and less frequent meetings. The state is also known for managing non-traditional risks like employee benefits.

min_capital.Requirement: Adheres to EU Solvency II framework

tax_notes: Transparent tax regime; Freedom of Service (FoS) access

name: Isle of Man
summary: The Isle of Man Financial Services Authority licenses captives as Class 12 insurers under the Insurance Act 2008 and the Insurance Regulations 2025, in operation from 30 June 2025. A Class 12 insurer may insure its own group, connected entities and connected individuals, and may reinsure a related customer only where a qualifying ceding insurer remains liable for the underlying claim. At 31 March 2025 the Authority reported 81 authorised Class 12 insurers. For non-life Class 12 business the minimum capital requirement is the higher of 75 percent of the solvency capital requirement and £100,000, and the fixed floor is £0 for a protected-cell-company cell. The solvency capital requirement for a non-dormant Class 12 insurer is a one-year value-at-risk at a 90 percent confidence level. The standard rate of Isle of Man corporate income tax is 0 percent. From 1 April 2026 the annual fee for a Class 12 authorised insurer is £8,565. A draft Class 12 and Class 13 valuation framework, consulted on in CP26-01, is written to come into operation on 31 December 2026 and is not in force.
legislation: Insurance Act 2008 and the Insurance Regulations 2025, with the Insurance (Non Long-Term Business Valuation and Solvency) Regulations 2021
applicable_legislation: Insurance Act 2008; Insurance Regulations 2025 (SD 2025/0138, in operation 30 June 2025), including Schedule 1 (Class 12 captive insurers), Schedule 2 (Class 13 insurance special purpose vehicles) and Schedule 3 (fast-track authorisation); Insurance (Non Long-Term Business Valuation and Solvency) Regulations 2021 (SD 2021/0274); Insurance (Long-Term Business Valuation and Solvency) Regulations 2021; Protected Cell Companies Act 2004; Incorporated Cell Companies Act 2010; Corporate Governance Code of Practice for Insurers 2021; Isle of Man Financial Services Authority (Fees) Order 2026 (SD 2026/0060, in operation 1 April 2026).

min_capital.Class 12, non-life, other than a PCC cel: The higher of 75 percent of the solvency capital requirement and £100,000. For a non-dormant Class 12 insurer the SCR is the one-year value-at-risk of basic own-funds at a 90 percent confidence level. Applies to Class 12 contracts within classes 3 to 9 and 11 (Insurance (Non Long-Term Business Valuation and Solvency) Regulations 2021, regulations 23 and 70)
min_capital.Class 12 protected cell company cell: The fixed floor is £0, so the minimum capital requirement equals 75 percent of the solvency capital requirement (regulation 70). This is the in-force rule. The draft regulations proposed to operate on 31 December 2026 would state a cell MCR of £0 and are not in force
min_capital.Class 12 dormant insurer: The minimum capital requirement equals the solvency capital requirement. For a dormant insurer that requirement is the regulatory capital needed so that assets exceed liabilities, including operational-management and regulatory-compliance liabilities
min_capital.Class 12 long-term business: Long-term Class 12 contracts, within classes 1, 2 and 10, are covered by the Insurance (Long-Term Business Valuation and Solvency) Regulations 2021 rather than the non-life floor above. A separate sterling floor for that long-term business was not located in the materials reviewed
min_capital.Class 13 insurance special purpose vehic: Must be fully funded at all times, with total adjusted net assets covering maximum aggregate exposure (Insurance Regulations 2025, Schedule 2). Class 13 is supplemental and does not by itself authorise insurance business. No separate fixed sterling floor was extracted

tax_notes: The Isle of Man Income Tax Division states that the standard rate of income tax for corporate taxpayers is 0 percent. A 10 percent rate, increased to 15 percent in the circumstances the Division describes for large multinational groups, applies to banking business and to Isle of Man retail business with taxable income above £500,000. A 20 percent rate applies to income from Isle of Man land and property and, from 6 April 2024, to petroleum extraction. Insurance is not one of those categories. No premium-tax rate is set in the Authority's Fees Order. The regulatory charge is the annual fee.

Class 12 protected cell companies and cells
Class 12 incorporated cell companies and cells
Class 13 insurance special purpose vehicles, which must also hold another class

There is no volume band on the Class 12 annual fee.
fees.premium_tax_rate: None. The standard corporate income-tax rate is 0 percent. The regulatory charge is the annual fee in the Fees Order 2026.

The annual regulatory return is submitted at the same time and includes the regulatory balance sheet, solvency capital requirement and minimum capital requirement, supplementary information, and a directors' certificate signed by two directors, at least one of whom is resident in the Island (Insurance Regulations 2025, regulation 19). A Class 12 insurer also submits a bi-annual return within three months after each six-month reporting period, unless the Authority approves another frequency. Class 12 insurers do not file the quarterly return required of other classes.

The Authority has not published a standard number of days for that process.
