name: Jersey
summary: Jersey has a growing reputation as an alternative location that follows international IAIS standards rather than Solvency II. The market has grown by over 30% in recent years due to an 'open for business' approach and the capability to handle both long and short-term risks. The JFSC maintains the discretion to amend capital requirements based on business projections.
tax_notes: Solvency margin at 17.5% of net premium for general business

name: Kansas
summary: Kansas law provides for pure, association, branch, and special purpose captives, with specific reporting requirements due by March 1 each year. Association captives can utilize letters of credit from state-chartered banks for capital requirements. The domicile leverages the NAIC Uniform Certificate of Authority for admission documents.
tax_notes: Tax paid on all premiums received on risks in the state

name: Kazakhstan
summary: The Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) is a unique hub that offers incentives to attract Kazakhstani capital and assets back from foreign jurisdictions. It provides three captive classes and utilizes a specific formula to calculate the premium risk component of capital. The jurisdiction is noted for its relocation-friendly regime, exemplified by the move of the Kazakhstan Energy Reinsurance Company from Bermuda.
legislation: AIFC Insurance and Reinsurance Prudential Rules
tax_notes: Friendly tax regime and operational incentives

name: Kentucky
summary: Kentucky is an established midwestern domicile that has grown to over 80 licensed captives across diverse industries like healthcare, banking, and manufacturing. It features a dedicated staff and graduated premium tax rates that become lower as premium volumes rise. A minimum annual tax of $5,000 is required if regular premium taxes fall below that threshold.
tax_notes: $5,000 minimum annual premium tax

name: Labuan
summary: Labuan IBFC is Asia's premier international financial hub, uniquely offering shariah-compliant Islamic captives, known as takaful captives. It is a substance-enabling jurisdiction with access to Malaysia's network of over 70 double taxation treaties. Every captive must have an operational office in Labuan or appoint a licensed underwriting manager.
legislation: Labuan Islamic Financial Services and Securities Act 2010

min_capital.Requirement: Risk-commensurate working funds in a Labuan bank

tax_notes: Fiscal neutrality and certainty

name: Liechtenstein
summary: Liechtenstein offers an adept workforce and unique central European access to both the EU and Switzerland markets. Captives are subject to Solvency II and can insure subsidiaries across the European Economic Area and third countries. While it does not tax capital, it applies a flat 12.5% tax rate on taxable income.
tax_notes: 12.5% flat tax on income; CHF 30,000 license fee

name: Luxembourg
summary: Luxembourg authorises captive insurance undertakings and captive reinsurance undertakings under the Law of 7 December 2015 on the insurance sector, as amended, and the Commissariat aux Assurances supervises them. The Law of 21 July 2021 moved the grant and withdrawal of authorisation from the Minister to the CAA. A reinsurance undertaking must be effectively run by at least one natural-person reinsurance executive, or by a CAA-authorised reinsurance management company represented by such an executive. In CAA Regulation 15/03, consolidated at 27 January 2023, the absolute floor of the minimum capital requirement is EUR 1,300,000 for a captive reinsurer and EUR 3,900,000 for any other reinsurer. Captive insurers use the ordinary insurance floors: EUR 2,700,000 for non-life, EUR 4,000,000 where liability classes 10 to 15 are covered, and EUR 4,000,000 for life. At 1 July 2026 the CAA reported 207 Luxembourg-law reinsurance undertakings and a total staff of 93. It does not publish a captive-only census or a captive-unit headcount. It described 12 new reinsurance authorisations in 2025 and 3 in the first half of 2026 as confirming renewed interest in reinsurance captives. Corporate income tax, in the income-tax law in force at 1 January 2026, is 14 percent up to EUR 175,000 of taxable income and 16 percent above EUR 200,000.
legislation: Law of 7 December 2015 on the insurance sector, as amended (consolidated text as of 3 April 2026), and Commissariat aux Assurances Regulation No. 15/03 of 7 December 2015, as amended
applicable_legislation: Law of 7 December 2015 on the insurance sector, as amended, including the definitions of captive insurance undertaking and captive reinsurance undertaking and Article 112 on the minimum capital requirement (CAA English consolidation as of 3 April 2026); Law of 21 July 2021, which transferred authorisation from the Minister to the CAA; CAA Regulation No. 15/03 of 7 December 2015 on insurance and reinsurance undertakings, as amended (English consolidation as of 27 January 2023, Article 52); Grand-Ducal Regulation of 5 December 2007 on the authorisation and exercise of reinsurance undertakings, as amended, on the provision pour fluctuation de sinistralité; CAA Circular 22/10 on annual reinsurance reporting; Grand-Ducal Regulation of 28 April 2014, as amended by the Grand-Ducal Regulation of 19 December 2020, on contributions to CAA staff and operating costs; amended Law of 4 December 1967 on income tax, Articles 167 and 174 (coordinated text in force at 1 January 2026).

min_capital.Captive reinsurance undertaking: Absolute floor of the minimum capital requirement EUR 1,300,000 (CAA Regulation 15/03, Article 52(2)(c), consolidation of 27 January 2023)
min_capital.Non-life insurance, including a captive: Absolute floor EUR 2,700,000, or EUR 4,000,000 where any risk in classes 10 to 15 of Annex I, Part A, of the 2015 law is covered (Article 52(2)(a))
min_capital.MCR relative to the SCR: The minimum capital requirement must not fall below 25 percent, and must not exceed 45 percent, of the solvency capital requirement including any capital add-on (Article 52(3)). It is calculated at least quarterly

tax_notes: Captive insurers and reinsurers are taxed as companies. Article 174 of the amended Law of 4 December 1967, in the Administration des contributions directes coordinated text in force at 1 January 2026, sets corporate income tax at 14 percent where taxable income does not exceed EUR 175,000, at EUR 24,500 plus 30 percent of the income above EUR 175,000 where taxable income is between EUR 175,000 and EUR 200,001, and at 16 percent above EUR 200,000. Guichet.lu, updated 7 April 2026, states that a further 7 percent of the corporate income tax is charged for the employment fund. The rate table on that Guichet page still describes the 2019 schedule of 15 and 17 percent and was not used for the rates above. Article 167 allows deduction of technical-provision allocations by insurance and reinsurance undertakings to the extent they correspond to obligations owed to insureds at the year-end, on conditions set by grand-ducal regulation. Every reinsurance undertaking must also constitute a provision pour fluctuation de sinistralité under the Grand-Ducal Regulation of 5 December 2007, as amended. The texts reviewed do not state, as a captive-specific rule, that this fluctuation provision is deductible in full. Municipal business tax and net wealth tax also apply; commune rates and the net-wealth tariff were not verified here. No premium-tax rate was found in the 2015 insurance-sector law materials reviewed.

fees.licensing_incorporation: No fixed captive application fee is stated on the CAA laws or regulations pages reviewed. The CAA annual report for 2025-2026 says staff and operating costs, other than retired-staff pensions, are met by taxes paid by supervised undertakings and by a state grant. Those taxes are set by the Grand-Ducal Regulation of 28 April 2014, as amended by the Grand-Ducal Regulation of 19 December 2020. The euro schedule in that regulation was not extracted in this verification.
fees.annual_fees: Annual contributions to CAA staff and operating costs are set by the Grand-Ducal Regulation of 28 April 2014, as amended on 19 December 2020. A current euro amount for a captive or reinsurance undertaking was not extracted from that regulation.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium-tax rate is set in the Law of 7 December 2015 materials reviewed. Corporate income tax applies under Article 174 of the income-tax law, at 14 percent up to EUR 175,000 of taxable income and 16 percent above EUR 200,000, plus the 7 percent employment-fund charge stated by Guichet.lu.

annual_filing_requirements: Insurance and reinsurance undertakings calculate the minimum capital requirement at least quarterly and report it to the CAA (Regulation 15/03, Article 52(4)). Reinsurance undertakings file an annual report. Circular 22/10 requires the claims-fluctuation-provision ceiling table, and the components of the annual movement where the provision exceeds 30 percent of the theoretical maximum. The 2025-2026 annual report says Circular 24/3, as modified by Circulars 25/5 and 25/6, splits the statutory auditor's separate report for reinsurance undertakings into a distinct report and a complementary distinct report, with different submission dates. Those day-counts were not extracted from the circulars. A change in ownership of a captive insurer or a reinsurance undertaking is notified on the forms introduced by Circular 24/9.
licensing_speed: No published standard authorisation timeline. The CAA examines the financial and organisational conditions, including human resources, before it grants an authorisation.

name: Malta
summary: Malta is the only EU member state with protected cell company (PCC) legislation that extends to brokers and insurance managers beyond traditional insurers. Its PCCs offer unique shared economies of scale and direct access to the EU market, effectively reducing fronting costs. The domicile is Fitch A+ rated and focuses on facilitating blockchain technology and legal certainty for smart contracts.
tax_notes: Direct access to UK and EU markets

name: Mauritius
summary: Mauritius is an emerging African domicile that provides stability with no exchange controls and an innovative pool of financial products. New proposed rules distinguish four classes of captive business based on the percentage of gross written premium originating from affiliates. Minimum unimpaired paid-up capital starts at approximately $86,750 for pure captives.
tax_notes: Long-standing bilateral relations with Africa

name: Michigan
summary: Michigan licenses a wide range of captives, including non-profit pure and special purpose financial captives. It maintains a strict resident requirement where two out of three organizers must be state residents, and board meetings must be held in-state. Notably, the state does not have a premium tax rate, using a renewal fee based on premium volume instead.
tax_notes: No tax rate; premium-volume based renewal fee

name: Missouri
summary: Centrally located with major non-stop flight access, Missouri emphasizes cost-reduction by using expert in-house analysts rather than outside consultants. It licenses varied structures, including special purpose life and sponsored cell captives. Application and licensing fees are deductible, helping to lower the barrier for new formations.
tax_notes: Direct tax rates tiered (0.38% down to 0.072%)

name: Montana
summary: Montana is recognized for having accessible regulators and one of the few regimes that offers special purpose captives under a series limited liability structure. This allows smaller captives to form with capital based on premium writing rather than a fixed minimum. The state legislature is extremely supportive, and captives are subject to mandatory examination at least every five years.
tax_notes: $5,000 minimum; $100,000 maximum tax

name: Netherlands
summary: The Dutch regulator, De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB), offers a robust supervision framework and has a deep understanding of captive-specific characteristics. Popular with Asian and American holding companies, the domicile has a local community of owners that evaluate supervisory topics. It is home to both insurance and reinsurance captives and features an exceptionally well-educated, English-speaking workforce.
tax_notes: Robust supervision framework

name: Nevada
summary: Nevada is one of the oldest US domiciles and frequently ranks first in new business launches due to its lack of corporate or personal income taxes. In 2019, it added a dormant captive status, allowing inactive companies to retain their certificate with fewer compliance requirements. Examination fees were also recently reduced by 33% to remain competitive.
tax_notes: $175,000 maximum tax; first-year credit up to $5,000

name: Nevis
summary: Nevis has provided a well-regulated international jurisdiction since 2004, geared toward the long-term viability of captives. It offers a low-cost environment with no tax on premiums, assets, or net income. Captives are formed as corporations but have a 'menu' of legal ownership options including trusts and LLCs to align with parent structures.
tax_notes: No tax paid on premiums, income, or assets

name: New Jersey
summary: New Jersey is an accessible domicile for Fortune 500 companies, regulated by the DOBI commissioner who actively seeks to modernize the market. The state enacted its legislation in 2011 and requires captives to hold at least one board meeting in the state per year. The commissioner holds discretionary authority to increase capital requirements based on the volume and nature of insurance.
tax_notes: $200,000 maximum annual tax

name: New Zealand
summary: New Zealand does not have specific captive-only legislation, instead governing all insurance through the IPSA 2010 act. Captives are explicitly exempt from the financial strength rating requirements that apply to traditional insurers. To obtain a license, a captive must demonstrate 'fitness for business' and the capacity to manage its specific risks.
tax_notes: Captives with no NZ business may fall outside IPSA scope

name: North Carolina
summary: North Carolina enacted the Captive Insurance Act in 2013 (Session Law 2013-116), now Part 9 of Article 10 of Chapter 58 of the General Statutes, and regulates captives through the Department of Insurance Captive Insurance Companies Division. At year-end 2025 the Department reported 263 captive insurance companies and 746 cells and series, including conditional licenses and approvals, for more than 1,000 risk-bearing entities. Those 263 companies were 188 pure captives, 48 protected cell captives, 9 risk retention groups, and 18 special purpose captives. During 2025 the state licensed 21 captive insurers, counting new formations and redomestications, and approved approximately 80 cells and series. Statutory capital floors are $250,000 for pure, protected cell, and special purpose captives, or another amount the Commissioner sets; $500,000 for association and industrial insured captives; $1,000,000 for a risk retention group; and $250,000 in cash for a special purpose financial captive. Direct premium tax is 0.4% on the first $20 million and 0.3% above that. The ordinary minimum is $5,000 and the ordinary maximum is $100,000. The redomestication premium-tax holiday expired for taxable years beginning on or after 1 January 2026.
legislation: North Carolina Captive Insurance Act (Chapter 58, Article 10, Part 9 of the General Statutes)
applicable_legislation: North Carolina General Statutes Chapter 58, Article 10, Part 9 (Captive Insurance Companies), enacted by Session Law 2013-116 and amended by Session Laws 2014-65, 2015-99, 2016-78, 2018-120, 2022-7, and 2024-29. Capital and surplus are in G.S. 58-10-370. Special purpose financial captive capital is in G.S. 58-10-575 and the application fee is in G.S. 58-10-565. Annual reports are in G.S. 58-10-405 and the annual audit is in G.S. 58-10-415. Inactive captives are in G.S. 58-10-490. The captive premium tax is G.S. 105-228.4A.

min_capital.Pure: Not less than $250,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus, or another amount determined by the Commissioner (G.S. 58-10-370(a)(1)).
min_capital.Association: Not less than $500,000 (G.S. 58-10-370(a)(2)). The Commissioner may prescribe additional capital.
min_capital.Industrial insured: Not less than $500,000 (G.S. 58-10-370(a)(3)). The Commissioner may prescribe additional capital.
min_capital.Risk retention group: Not less than $1,000,000 (G.S. 58-10-370(a)(4)). The Commissioner may prescribe additional capital.
min_capital.Protected cell: Not less than $250,000, or another amount determined by the Commissioner (G.S. 58-10-370(a)(5)).
min_capital.Special purpose: Not less than $250,000, or another amount determined by the Commissioner (G.S. 58-10-370(a)(6)).
min_capital.Special purpose financial captive: Not less than $250,000 of initial capital, all in cash. The Commissioner may require additional capital after reviewing the plan of operation, feasibility study, pro formas, and the risks insured or reinsured (G.S. 58-10-575).
min_capital.Branch captive: A branch captive is a pure captive for its North Carolina operations unless the Commissioner permits otherwise (G.S. 58-10-340). As security for branch liabilities it must hold an amount equal to the pure-captive minimum plus reserves on branch business, with a credit the Commissioner may allow for security already posted (G.S. 58-10-535).
min_capital.Inactive captive: Unimpaired capital and surplus in an amount determined by the Commissioner (G.S. 58-10-490). A risk retention group cannot be declared inactive.
min_capital.Form of capital: Cash, securities approved by the Commissioner, a clean irrevocable letter of credit from a bank the Commissioner approves, or another approved form (G.S. 58-10-370(c)). Special purpose financial captive minimum initial capital must be cash.

tax_notes: G.S. 105-228.4A taxes a North Carolina captive, and taxes only the branch business of a branch captive. A foreign captive is not subject to this tax. Direct premiums, after return premiums, are taxed at 0.4% up to $20 million and 0.3% above $20 million. Assumed reinsurance premiums are taxed at 0.225% up to $20 million, 0.150% from $20 million to $40 million, 0.050% from $40 million to $60 million, and 0.025% above $60 million. Assumed-reinsurance tax does not apply to risks already taxed as direct premiums, or to a qualifying assumption of reserves between commonly controlled insurers that is part of a plan to discontinue one insurer. For any captive other than the multi-cell case below, the tax is at least $5,000 and at most $100,000. A protected cell captive with more than 10 cells, or a special purpose captive with a cell or series structure of more than 10 cells or series, pays at least $10,000 and at most the lesser of $100,000 plus $5,000 for each cell or series over 10, and $200,000. Two or more captives under common ownership and control are taxed as one captive, except a protected cell captive and a special purpose captive with a cell or series structure. The premium-tax report and payment are due by March 15. Captives subject to this tax are not subject to the franchise tax, to income tax except as G.S. 105-130.5A provides, to local privilege or local gross-premium taxes, or to the insurance regulatory charge. The redomestication holiday in G.S. 105-228.4A(g) expired for taxable years beginning on or after 1 January 2026. An inactive captive is not liable for tax under Article 8B of Chapter 105 for any full year it is inactive (G.S. 58-10-490).
contact_name: Lori Gorman, Deputy Commissioner, Captive Insurance Companies Division
types_allowed: Special purpose captive insurance companies, including cell or series structures
Inactive captive insurance companies declared by the Commissioner, other than risk retention groups

fees.licensing_incorporation: The Department states that it charges no captive fees except the special purpose financial captive application review. Under G.S. 58-10-565(h), when the Department uses internal resources that review has a minimum fee of $12,000, of which $6,000 is payable on filing and the remainder on licensure. The cost of outside legal, financial, and audit services may also be charged to the applicant. Corporate organization fees are paid to the North Carolina Secretary of State and are not set in the Captive Insurance Act.
fees.annual_fees: No North Carolina Department of Insurance annual captive license or renewal fee is published. The Department's stated exception to its no-fee practice is the special purpose financial captive application review described above, which is not an annual fee.
fees.premium_tax_rate: Direct premiums: 0.4% up to $20 million and 0.3% above $20 million. Assumed reinsurance premiums: 0.225% up to $20 million, 0.150% from $20 million to $40 million, 0.050% from $40 million to $60 million, and 0.025% above $60 million. Ordinary minimum $5,000 and ordinary maximum $100,000. A protected cell captive with more than 10 cells, or a special purpose captive with more than 10 cells or series, has a $10,000 minimum and a maximum of the lesser of $100,000 plus $5,000 per cell or series over 10, and $200,000. The redomestication tax holiday expired for taxable years beginning on or after 1 January 2026.

annual_filing_requirements: Each captive submits a report of its financial condition as of the preceding December 31, verified by two executive officers, before March 15. Reporting is on generally accepted accounting principles unless the Commissioner requires or accepts another basis (G.S. 58-10-405). A pure, special purpose, or industrial insured captive may be allowed to file 75 days after its fiscal year-end. The annual audit and statement of actuarial opinion for captives other than risk retention groups are due by June 30, or within 180 days after an approved fiscal year-end (G.S. 58-10-415). Risk retention groups file under Parts 6 and 7 of Article 10 instead of that audit section. The premium-tax report and payment are due by March 15 (G.S. 105-228.4A). The Department's filing page for 2026 also lists Form C-202, the direct economic impact supplement, and Form C-207 for inactive captives. Filings are submitted electronically through the Department's online system or to the Captive Insurance Administrator. The Commissioner may waive the annual report if the annual audit is filed, and may grant a hardship exemption from the audit, but may not waive both at the same time. A request to skip the annual report is due at least 30 days before the report due date.
licensing_speed: No published standard licensing turnaround. The Commissioner may grant provisional approval for not more than 90 days under G.S. 58-10-347 and may extend it in 30-day increments for good cause.

regulator.name: North Carolina Department of Insurance, Captive Insurance Companies Division
regulator.address: 3200 Beechleaf Court, Raleigh, NC 27604. Mailing address: 1203 Mail Service Center, Raleigh, NC 27699-1203

name: Oklahoma
summary: Oklahoma is recognized for continuous innovation, offering competitive arrays of investment options and a provisional license for new applicants and redomestications. In 2020, it introduced an incentive for 'Series' captives to maintain only $50,000 in capital if certain risk-segregation criteria are met. Captives are permitted to conduct a broad selection of coverages, including workers' compensation.
tax_notes: 0.2% direct / 0.1% assumed rates; $100,000 cap

name: Oregon
summary: Oregon describes itself as a business-friendly domicile that collaboratively forms captives for financial success and legal compliance. A notable attribute is that Oregon does not collect any premium tax, charging only a flat initial and annual renewal fee. All captives are examined at least once every three years by the Division of Financial Regulation.
tax_notes: No premium tax; $5,000 annual renewal fee

name: Panama
summary: Captive insurance in Panama is subject to Law 60 of 1996, which distinguishes between long-term life risks and general risks. In Panama, local risks are generally not insurable; the law focuses on foreign risks managed from a physically identified office in Panama. Obtaining a license is a two-stage process involving legal vehicle registration followed by a superintendent license request.
tax_notes: $2,000 annual service fee

name: Puerto Rico
summary: Puerto Rico offers a unique 'dual sovereignty' environment, governed by standard US federal oversight while Puerto Rican law takes precedence in corporate and insurance matters. It maintains an International Insurance Center as a one-stop regulatory shop for over 450 active captives. Pure captives utilize a 5:1 premium to surplus ratio, while association captives cap third-party risks at 20%.
tax_notes: Preferred tax environment; Class-based application fees

name: Singapore
summary: After licensing its first captive in 1983, Singapore has grown into the largest Asia Pacific captive domicile and a major reinsurance center. It is governed by the Insurance Act and offers chargeable income tax exemptions of up to SGD 152,500. Capital adequacy is set strictly such that equity and retained earnings must exceed the sum of SGD 400,000 and calculated insurance fund components.
tax_notes: 17% corporate rate with 10% concessionary rate for qualifying activity

name: South Carolina
summary: South Carolina has licensed captive insurers since the enabling law of 2000, now Title 38, Chapter 90 of the Code of Laws, and supervises them through the Department of Insurance Captive Insurance Division. The Division reported 235 active captive insurance companies as of February 2026 and 15 new licenses in 2025. A pure captive must hold at least $250,000. An industrial insured captive or a risk retention group must hold at least $500,000, and an association captive at least $750,000. A special purpose financial captive's minimum initial capital is $250,000 in cash. Sponsored captives, and special purpose captives that are not risk retention groups, have capital set by the director. Direct premium tax is 0.4% on the first $20 million and 0.3% after that. Assumed-reinsurance tax steps from 0.225% down to 0.025%. The combined tax has a $5,000 minimum, prorated in the year a captive is first licensed, and a $100,000 maximum. After a completed application, the Division expects licensing to take 30 to 45 days, with additional time possible for a special purpose financial captive.
legislation: South Carolina Code of Laws, Title 38, Chapter 90 (Captive Insurance Companies)
applicable_legislation: South Carolina Code of Laws Title 38, Chapter 90, originating in 2000 Act No. 331 and including 2018 Act No. 251 and 2025 Act Nos. 42 and 62. Capitalization is §38-90-40. Licensing and the ordinary fee are §38-90-20. Annual reports are §38-90-70. Premium tax is §38-90-140. Special purpose financial captives are Article 3 of the chapter, including capitalization in §38-90-460, fees in §38-90-440, and tax in §38-90-580.

min_capital.Pure: Not less than $250,000 of free and unimpaired paid-in capital, surplus, unrestricted net assets of a nonprofit, or a combination (S.C. Code §38-90-40(A)(1)(a)).
min_capital.Association: Not less than $750,000 for an association captive incorporated as a stock insurer or mutual insurer, or organized as a limited liability company (§38-90-40(A)(1)(b)).
min_capital.Sponsored: An amount determined by the director after considering the business plan, feasibility study, and pro formas, including the nature, scale, and complexity of the risks (§38-90-40(A)(1)(d)). The Division's types page states the same case-by-case standard.
min_capital.Special purpose: For a special purpose captive that is not a risk retention group, an amount determined by the director on the same business-plan basis as a sponsored captive (§38-90-40(A)(1)(e)).
min_capital.Special purpose financial captive: Not less than $250,000. All of the minimum initial capitalization must be cash. The director may require additional capital (S.C. Code §38-90-460).
min_capital.Branch captive: Section 38-90-40(C) requires a United States trust, funded by an irrevocable letter of credit or other acceptable asset, of not less than the reserves on policies and reinsurance written through the branch, with a credit the director may allow for security already posted with a reinsurer or fronting company. The Division's types page separately lists a $250,000 statutory minimum for a branch captive under §38-90-40.
min_capital.Additional capital: The director may prescribe additional capital and surplus based on the type, volume, and nature of business to be transacted (§38-90-40(A)(2)). Required capital is held as cash, approved securities, a clean irrevocable letter of credit, or another form the director approves.

tax_notes: Under S.C. Code §38-90-140, tax is paid to the Department by March 1. Direct premiums, after return premiums, are taxed at 0.4% on the first $20 million and 0.3% on each dollar after that. Assumed reinsurance premiums are taxed at 0.225% on the first $20 million, 0.150% on the next $20 million, 0.050% on the next $20 million, and 0.025% after that. Reinsurance tax does not apply to risks already taxed on a direct basis, or to a qualifying assumption of reserves under common ownership and control that is part of a plan to discontinue the cedent's related operations. If the direct and assumed taxes together are under $5,000, the captive pays a $5,000 minimum. In the calendar year of first licensure that minimum is prorated by quarter: $5,000, $3,750, $2,500, or $1,250. If the calculated taxes exceed $100,000, the captive pays a $100,000 maximum. Captives under common ownership and control are taxed as separate companies. For a branch captive the tax applies only to branch business. For a sponsored captive, the sponsored captive and its incorporated and unincorporated protected cells are taxed on a consolidated basis as one captive. This tax is in lieu of other occupation taxes, except ad valorem taxes on real and personal property used in producing income. A special purpose financial captive is taxed under §38-90-580 at the same direct and assumed rates, with its own $5,000 minimum and $100,000 maximum, and each of its protected cells is taxed as a separate special purpose financial captive. The Division's fee schedule publishes the same $5,000 minimum and $100,000 maximum.
types_allowed: Sponsored captive insurance companies, with incorporated or unincorporated protected cells

fees.licensing_incorporation: For a captive other than a special purpose financial captive, S.C. Code §38-90-20 sets a nonrefundable $200 application-processing fee and a $300 license fee for the year of registration. The director may also charge the reasonable cost of outside legal, financial, and examination services. The Division's published schedule lists a $4,000 review fee for those captives and a $0 processing fee beside the $200 application fee. For a special purpose financial captive, §38-90-440 sets a $200 processing fee, a minimum $12,000 fee when internal resources examine the application ($6,000 on filing and the remainder on licensure) or the cost of outside services, and a $300 initial license fee. The Division schedule lists that application fee as $12,000.
fees.annual_fees: Annual renewal license fee of $500 for captives and for special purpose financial captives (§§38-90-20 and 38-90-440). A special purpose financial captive also pays an annual review fee of $2,400, or the actual cost if the director determines that cost is higher.
fees.premium_tax_rate: Direct premiums: 0.4% on the first $20 million and 0.3% thereafter. Assumed reinsurance premiums: 0.225% on the first $20 million, 0.150% on the next $20 million, 0.050% on the next $20 million, and 0.025% thereafter. Combined minimum $5,000, prorated by quarter in the year of first licensure, and combined maximum $100,000. A special purpose financial captive is taxed at the same rates under §38-90-580, and each of its protected cells is taxed separately. Due March 1.

annual_filing_requirements: A risk retention group submits its annual report by March 1. Every other captive submits its annual report by July 1. The report is verified by two executive officers and uses generally accepted accounting principles unless the director approves statutory accounting principles (S.C. Code §38-90-70). A non-risk-retention captive with a fiscal year-end other than December 31 files its income statement and premium schedule before March 1 and the full annual report within 180 days after fiscal year-end. Premium tax is due March 1 (§38-90-140). Beginning the year after licensure, the board, the managing board of a limited liability company, or the subscribers' advisory committee of a reciprocal must meet at least annually with a quorum physically present in South Carolina, including at least two members physically present in the state (§38-90-20). The Division's filing calendar also sets June 30 for the non-risk-retention actuarial opinion and audited financial statements, and it sets quarterly statements and NAIC-style filings for risk retention groups and special purpose financial captives.
licensing_speed: 30 to 45 days after receipt of a completed application, depending on complexity. Special purpose financial captives may require additional review time.

regulator.name: South Carolina Department of Insurance, Captive Insurance Division
regulator.address: 1201 Main Street, Suite 1000, Columbia, SC 29201. Charleston office: 145 King Street, Suite 228, Charleston, SC 29401

name: South Dakota
summary: South Dakota is nationally recognized for user-friendly trust laws and a common-sense regulatory environment where owners work directly with decision makers. It does not charge premium taxes, opting instead for a supervision fee that can never exceed $50,000 annually. Captives must maintain their principal place of business and hold at least one board meeting in the state with a physical quorum.
tax_notes: No premium tax; supervision fee capped at $50,000

name: St Lucia
summary: St Lucia requires all insurance applications to be conducted through an international business company (IBC) with a local registered agent and office. The FSRA maintains the discretion to fix solvency margins and guidelines distinguish between Class A, B, and C licenses based on risk type. IBC structures generally enjoy tax-neutral status unless they elect for a 1% tax.
tax_notes: No tax unless 1% election is made; special confidentiality provisions

name: Switzerland
summary: Switzerland boasts top-tier political and fiscal stability, with major insurance hubs in Zurich and Zug offering a vast pool of experienced staff. Captives benefit from proportional regulation and relief from tied-asset regulations for intra-group activities. The Swiss Solvency Test (SST) is basically parallel to EU requirements, offering simplified models for reinsurance captives.

min_capital.Requirement: FINMA prescribed; takes less than one year to comply

tax_notes: OECD compliant tax levels; many cantons have lowered corporate tax

name: Tennessee
summary: Tennessee was one of the first onshore US domiciles and has grown to rank in the top 20 globally after modernizing its statute in 2011. It is one of the few states that allows series limited liability companies, offering lower administrative burdens for incorporated cells. The state even offers a one-year tax holiday for alien captives redomesticating to Tennessee.
tax_notes: $5,000 minimum tax; tiered rates with $100,000 max

name: Texas
summary: Texas focuses on single-parent captives to help business owners protect the enterprise value they create. While primarily supportive of single-parent structures, the state seeks to create the most broadly constructive statute possible for this category. The Texas Department of Insurance examines actuarial projections and other issues before finalizing any formation decisions.
tax_notes: 0.5% premium tax; $7,500 min / $200,000 max

name: The Bahamas
summary: The Bahamas licenses captives as restricted external insurers under the External Insurance Act, 2009 (Chapter 348), supervised by the Insurance Commission of The Bahamas. A restricted external insurer may cover its members, subsidiaries and affiliates, reinsureds who acknowledge in writing that it is restricted, and other persons the Commission approves. Unrestricted external insurers may write broader business from The Bahamas. Cell programmes use segregated accounts companies under the Segregated Accounts Companies Act (Chapter 369C). The Commission does not publish a current captive or external-insurer census; the statistics page covers domestic general and long-term business, and the latest files there run through 2022. Capital for a restricted insurer is the amount the Commission approves. The prescribed floors for unrestricted insurers are B$100,000 for general business, B$200,000 for long-term business and B$300,000 for both. The annual licence fee is B$2,500 for a restricted insurer and B$3,500 for an unrestricted insurer. Section 52 of the Act gives a licensed external insurer a 20-year exemption, running from the date of its first licence, from Bahamian taxes, fees, duties and imposts other than provisions of that kind already in force when the Act commenced and other than licence charges under the Act. Audited financial statements are due within four months of the financial year-end. The Commission has posted a Draft External Insurance Act, 2025; this profile follows the 2009 Act and the 2010 regulations.

applicable_legislation: External Insurance Act, 2009 (Chapter 348); External Insurance (Capital Requirements for External Insurers, Insurance Managers and External Insurance Brokers) Regulations, 2010; External Insurance (Forms and Fees) Regulations, 2010; External Insurance (Classes of Insurance Business) Regulations, 2010; External Insurance (Variable Insurance Business) Regulations, 2010; Segregated Accounts Companies Act (Chapter 369C). The Insurance Commission also publishes a Draft External Insurance Act, 2025, which is not treated as in force here.

min_capital.Restricted external insurer (captive): Paid-up capital or contributed reserve in the amount approved by the Commission, in cash or other approved assets (External Insurance Act, 2009, s.22(2))

tax_notes: The External Insurance Act does not impose a premium tax. Section 52 exempts a licensed external insurer, for 20 years from the date of its first licence, from any tax, fee, duty or impost in The Bahamas, other than provisions of that kind in force when the Act commenced and other than amounts payable for a licence under the Act. The standing annual charge is the licence fee.

fees.licensing_incorporation: B$250 application for an external insurer licence; B$250 application for a segregated account of an external insurer; B$100 application for an insurance manager or external insurance broker. fees.annual_fees: Restricted external insurer B$2,500; unrestricted external insurer B$3,500; insurance manager B$1,000; external insurance broker B$1,000. Late payment adds 10, 15, 20 or 25 percent of the amount due, according to the quarterly ageing of the overdue fee.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax under the External Insurance Act. Section 52 provides a 20-year exemption from other Bahamian taxes, fees, duties and imposts, subject to the carve-outs in that section. The annual regulatory charge is the licence fee above.

annual_filing_requirements: Audited financial statements, complying with international accounting standards or another standard the Commission determines, are due within four months after the financial year-end, or any longer period the Commission allows. They must be audited by a Commission-approved auditor and accompanied by the auditor's report and by the auditor's certificate on the statutory books, compliance with the section 31 solvency test at the balance-sheet date, and compliance with anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing reporting. The Commission may also require an actuary's certificate that reserves are adequate. A licensee whose outstanding claims, including incurred-but-not-reported claims, exceed 200 percent of capital and surplus must file an annual actuarial review of those claims. A licensee incorporated outside The Bahamas must, within four months of year-end, file a certificate from its overseas regulator. Each licensee must maintain a resident representative in The Bahamas. The external-insurer licence is renewable annually.

name: Utah
summary: Utah licenses captives under the Utah Captive Insurance Companies Act, Title 31A, Chapter 37, administered by the Utah Insurance Department Captive Insurance Division. The chapter covers agency, association, branch, industrial insured, pooling, pure, risk retention group, sponsored, special purpose, and special purpose financial captives, and cells of a sponsored captive may be protected cells or incorporated cells. The Department's 2024 annual report, Table A, lists 373 captive insurers, 13 sponsored captive insurers, and 107 cells authorized to write insurance in Utah. The Department does not publish one combined total, and it has not published a 2025 annual report. A certificate of authority expires annually and is renewed by 1 July. The governing body meets at least once a year in Utah, with a quorum and at least one out-of-state individual physically present, unless the captive is a member of the Utah Captive Insurance Association at the highest membership level. The Division's benefits page states that a flat annual fee is charged in lieu of state premium tax. Real and personal property in Utah remains taxable.
legislation: Utah Captive Insurance Companies Act, Title 31A, Chapter 37, Utah Code
applicable_legislation: Title 31A, Chapter 37, Utah Code, including section 31A-37-102 (definitions), section 31A-37-201 (certificate of authority, in-state meeting or Utah Captive Insurance Association membership, and renewal by 1 July), and section 31A-37-204 (paid-in capital). The Division also cites section 31A-37-501 and rule R590-238 for the annual statement, economic-benefit statement, audit, and actuarial opinion. The current statutory text used here is the version effective 6 May 2026.

min_capital.Pure captive acting as a pool: Not less than USD $250,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital and unimpaired paid-in surplus (Utah Code section 31A-37-204(2)(a)(i)(A)).
min_capital.Pure captive that is not a pool: If the pure captive is not acting as a pool that facilitates risk distribution for other captive insurers, the greater of 20 percent of the company's total aggregate risk and USD $50,000 (section 31A-37-204(2)(a)(i)(B)). The Division's basics and benefits pages state a flat USD $250,000 for a pure captive and do not restate this alternative.
min_capital.Sponsored captive: Not less than USD $250,000, of which a minimum of USD $50,000 is provided by the sponsor (section 31A-37-204(2)(a)(iv)).
min_capital.Cell: Section 31A-37-204 does not set a cell floor. The Division's basics page states that a cell has no regulatory minimum and that the sponsor sets it.
min_capital.Special purpose captive: An amount determined by the commissioner after considering the business plan, feasibility study, and pro formas, including the nature of the risks to be insured (section 31A-37-204(2)(a)(v)).
min_capital.Agency, branch, and special purpose fina: Section 31A-37-102 includes these as captive insurance companies. Section 31A-37-204(2) does not state a separate dollar floor for them.
min_capital.Form of capital: Required paid-in capital and surplus may be cash or a cash equivalent, an irrevocable letter of credit that the commissioner approves and that is issued by a Utah-chartered bank, a Federal Reserve member bank, or an FDIC member bank, or marketable securities determined under section 31A-37-204(1). The commissioner may require additional capital based on the type, volume, and nature of the business.

tax_notes: The Division's benefits page states that a flat annual fee is charged in lieu of state premium taxes, and that real and personal property owned in Utah is taxed. The basics page states the same: no state taxes, with real and personal property taxes still applying. The annual captive fee published by the Division is USD $7,250 plus a USD $250 e-commerce fee, USD $7,500 in total, and USD $1,000 for a cell. No Utah corporate income tax on captives is stated on those pages.

fees.licensing_incorporation: Division basics page: USD $200 application submission fee; initial licence fee of USD $7,250 without proration (USD $1,000 for a cell); initial e-commerce fee of USD $250 without proration, not charged to a cell. Incorporation is a nominal fee paid to the Utah Department of Commerce.
fees.annual_fees: Annual renewal fee of USD $7,250 due before 1 June (USD $1,000 for a cell) and an annual e-commerce fee of USD $250 due before 1 June, not charged to a cell. The benefits page states the captive total as USD $7,500, including the e-commerce fee. The certificate of authority expires annually and is renewed by 1 July under section 31A-37-201(8).
fees.premium_tax_rate: No state premium tax. The Division charges the flat annual fee in lieu of state premium tax. Real and personal property taxes still apply.

annual_filing_requirements: The annual statement of financial condition is due before 1 March, verified under oath of two executive officers, and is filed on the Department portal. A statement of economic benefit to Utah is due before 1 March. An audited financial report and a statement of actuarial opinion are due on or before 30 June for the year ended 31 December. A risk retention group also files the applicable NAIC annual statement blank. There is no mandatory examination period. The commissioner may call an examination at any time, and a called examination typically covers the preceding five years, at the captive's cost. The governing body meets in Utah at least annually, unless the captive holds the highest level of Utah Captive Insurance Association membership.

name: Vermont
summary: Vermont is the largest onshore captive domicile in the United States and a premier global captive hub, having pioneered the US industry with the enactment of the Special Insurer Act of 1981 (8 V.S.A. Chapter 141). Regulated by the Vermont Department of Financial Regulation (DFR) Captive Insurance Division—which maintains a dedicated in-house team of analysts and financial examiners—and supported by the Vermont Captive Insurance Association (VCIA), the state had 707 licensed captives ($243.6B in assets and $36.3B in gross written premium) at year-end 2025, with 51 new licences and 27 dissolutions. Vermont licenses nine distinct captive structures, offers a 30-day licensing turnaround, and provides a competitive graduated premium tax capped at $200,000 with a $5,000 tax credit in each of the first two years.
